title: Bats May Have First Appeared in Europe, Study Says
summary:
Where did bats first appear? Scientists have argued about this for many years. Africa, Asia, and North America were all suggested as possible homes. Now a big international team says the answer may be Europe.

The team included 137 researchers from 64 countries. They worked through a project called Bat1K, which aims to read the genetic instructions, called genomes, of every living bat species. The study appeared in the journal Nature.

The scientists studied 103 bat genomes. Forty-two of these were newly built in great detail. The bats covered all 21 recognized bat families. The team also used evidence from 44 bat fossils, which are ancient remains preserved in rock.

Putting all this together, the researchers built a family tree of bats. It suggests bats first evolved in Europe during the late Paleocene, roughly 65 to 60 million years ago. Later, their descendants moved into Africa. Other groups spread to the Americas, Asia, and Australia.

Bats are unusual mammals. They are the only mammals that can truly fly with power, flapping their wings. Most bats can also find their way and hunt in the dark using sound, a skill called echolocation.

Bats make up about one fifth of all living mammals. Many are surprisingly resistant to disease and live much longer than other mammals of similar size.

The study also looked at a fossil bat called Vielasia. It sits on the oldest branch of the bat family tree. That fossil suggests echolocation had already appeared near the beginning of bat evolution. Together, the evidence hints that both powered flight and echolocation came before modern bat groups split apart.

"It is extraordinary, after decades of research and conflicting findings, we finally have a robust phylogenetic tree," said Professor Emma Teeling of University College Dublin, a leading senior author. She added that the genomes can help uncover how bats' special abilities work.

Teeling said the findings point to Europe as the most likely place where mammalian powered flight first evolved. Another senior author, Professor Liliana M. Dávalos of Stony Brook University, said the team's method can model fossil and living species together, which other methods cannot.
why_it_matters: Knowing where and when bats evolved helps scientists understand how mammals first learned to fly and how bats' special abilities developed.
